title: Chet
hook: with yud it spells chai, life

segments.voice: Yesterday, two words for the Sabbath, remember and keep, spoken as one. Your line: zayin remembers. Today, a letter you may already have heard at a party.

The speeches are over. Somebody's uncle talked a little too long, the bride's friend made everyone cry, and now the glasses go up: wine, whiskey, sparkling water, whatever's in hand. The whole table says one word together: l'chaim! Glasses touch. At Jewish weddings, at a bris, at a new job, even after a funeral when the family sits down to eat, that's the word. It means to life. And the word for life starts with a sound you make at the back of your throat.

You met l'chaim in year three, raised at tables after mourning; today, the letter inside it. First, its look. Chet is a cousin of heh, the breath letter. Heh has a small gap at the top left, as if air can still slip out. Chet closes the gap: two legs and a roof, sealed. The sound changes too: not an easy h, but breath pushed against the back of the throat, ch. Second, the word. Put chet beside a yud, a tiny hanging stroke, and you have chai: alive, living. Its plural, chayim, is the everyday word for life. L'chaim simply means to life. Third, a sentence that gives the word weight. Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses lays out the choice before the people. In the King James: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life." Not just enjoy it. Choose it, as if life were something you keep picking up, day after day. Fourth, a custom. Tradition gives each Hebrew letter a number, and says chet and yud together add up to eighteen. So some people give gifts in multiples of eighteen, and some wear chai on a chain around their neck. And l'chaim isn't only for weddings. Over coffee with a friend you haven't seen in a while, it's a way of noticing, out loud, that you're both still here.
screen: `HEH WITH THE GAP CLOSED.` · `CHET AND YUD: CHAI, ALIVE.` · `THEREFORE CHOOSE LIFE.` · `EIGHTEEN, TRADITION SAYS.` · then, large: `L'CHAIM: TO LIFE.`

segments.voice: Hold a cup if one is near, water or tea, anything, and bring to mind one thing in your life that's alive right now: a person, a friendship, a plant on the windowsill, a project finally growing. Lift the cup a little toward it, say l'chaim under your breath, and sip slowly; if you pray, give thanks for it.
Chet. The throaty letter that, with a yud beside it, spells chai: alive, life. Today's word.
Your line: chet for life. Life is something you can choose again. See you at tet.

howItsDone: At Jewish celebrations, from weddings to a meal after a hard day, people raise a glass and say l'chaim, 'to life'; some give gifts in multiples of eighteen, the number tradition assigns to chai, and some wear the word chai as a pendant.

original.note: Hebrew: alive, living; chet (ח) plus yud (י). The toast l'chaim (לְחַיִּים) means to life.

trapdoor: what you thought: chet is just the throaty ch sound.
what it means: with yud it spells chai, alive, the life in l'chaim.
what a scholar hears: by the tradition of letter values, ח and י make eighteen, and Deuteronomy 30:19 makes life a choice: "therefore choose life."

chat.says: Why do my Jewish friends give gifts like eighteen or thirty-six dollars?
options: Tradition says the letters of chai, alive, add up to eighteen. It's a gift of life.
Eighteen is the age of adulthood in the Torah, so it marks growing up.
It's an old tax amount from the Temple, kept as a lucky number.
chat.meaning: Tradition gives each letter a number, and chet and yud, which spell chai, add up to eighteen. So some give gifts in multiples of eighteen.
